text.p: These are some of the main stories in Sofia newspapers today. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- Bulgaria is expected to raise electricity prices by 30 percent from April 1, interim Energy minister Geogri Stoilov said.

-- Russia was ready to extend to Bulgaria $450 million loan with a four-year grace period and due to be repaid by the year 2010 for buying 14 Russian-made MIG-29 SM jet fighters, a senior official from the MIG-MAPO manufacturer said. @

-- Bulgaria's Agriculture minister Roumen Hristov said he had send a letter to the European Union (EU) agriculture commissioner Franz Fischler saying Bulgaria was ready to buy 100,000 tonnes of EU wheat at affordable prices. The purchases were to be paid for through a World Bank loan.
-- Bulgaria expects to receive some 85 million Ecus in 1997 under the EU's PHARE programme, deputy Foreign minister Valentin Dobrev said.

-- Bulgaria's state-owned Bulgargas is expected to raise to 33.5 percent from 25.1 percent its share in the Bulgarian-Russian joint stock company Topenergy by buying the stakes owned by Bulgaria's First Private Bank, Bulbank and Chimimport, Bulgargas executive director Vassil Filipov said. The Russian RAO Gazprom has a 50 percent stake in Topenergy.

-- Bulgaria's State Insurance Institute (SII) posted 11.2 billion levs revenue from insurance premiums last year, SII's chairman Maxim Sirakov said. SII's 1996 pre-tax profit was 1.2 billion levs and damages paid totalled some 7.7 billion levs.
-- The Sofia City Court is to rule on an insolvency case against the Private Agricultural and Investment Bank filed by the Bulgarian National Bank at the beginning of April, court officials said.
-- Bulgaria plans to set up a new tax service to monitor 600 biggest local taxpayers with an annual turnover over one billion levs each, deputy Finance minister Bisser Slavkov said.

-- Bulgaria's interim cabinet approved ammendments to the profit tax law which allow foreigners to pay corporate tax under Bulgaria's billateral agreements with their countries to avoid double taxation.

-- Bulgaria's President Petar Stoyanov appointed his economic advisor Krassimir Angarski as a minister without portfolio in the caretaker cabinet in charge of economic policy and relations with international lenders.
Angarski also headed the Bank Consolidation Company, which manages state equity in local commercial banks.
